title: ARM Assembly Programming
blurb: Write, trace, and debug ARM assembly using instructions, memory addressing, branches, stacks, functions, and exceptions.
description: A practical ARM assembly course focused on writing, tracing, and debugging ARMASM programs.

beginner: Instructions Part 1: syntax, MOV/MVN, memory addressing, barrel shifter
intermediate: Instructions Part 2: flags, comparisons, data processing, control flow, stacks
Functions: register saving and parameter passing
Exceptions: entry, vectors, priorities and SVC

lessons.title: ARMASM program structure & directives
lessons.explanation: Practice building a minimal ARMASM file: define the code area, mark the entry point, create aliases or constants, execute instructions, and end the source.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY; Declare code area
        ENTRY; Mark entry point
counter RN 0; Alias register r0 as counter
limit   EQU 5; Define symbolic constant limit
        MOV counter, #0; Initialize counter to 0
stop    B stop; Loop forever
        END; End of assembly
commonMistakes: Treating assembler directives such as AREA or EQU as instructions executed by the ARM core.
lessons.explain: Practice building a minimal ARMASM file: define the code area, mark the entry point, create aliases or constants, execute instructions, and end the source.

lessons.title: MOV, MVN & immediate operands
lessons.explanation: Practice loading immediate values, copying register values, and producing a bitwise complement with MOV and MVN.
examples:
MOV r0, #17; Load immediate value 17 into r0
        MOV r1, r0; Copy r0 into r1
        MVN r2, r1; Bitwise NOT of r1 into r2
commonMistakes: Reading MOV r0, r1 as copying r0 into r1.
lessons.explain: Practice loading immediate values, copying register values, and producing a bitwise complement with MOV and MVN.

lessons.title: LDR/STR & addressing practice
lessons.explanation: Practice loading and storing words, bytes, and halfwords while calculating base-plus-offset, pre-indexed, and post-indexed addresses.
examples:
MOV r2, #0x1000; Base pointer address
        MOV r0, #17; Initial test value 17
        STR r0, [r2]; Store word to memory
        MOV r0, #23; Second test value 23
        STR r0, [r2, #4]; Store word with offset 4
        LDR r1, [r2]; Load word from base
        LDR r3, [r2, #4]; Load word from offset 4
        STR r3, [r2, #8]; Store word to offset 8
        LDR r4, [r2], #4; Post-indexed load and advance pointer
commonMistakes: Confusing the address in the base register with the data loaded from memory.
lessons.explain: Practice loading and storing words, bytes, and halfwords while calculating base-plus-offset, pre-indexed, and post-indexed addresses.

lessons.title: Shift practice: LSL, LSR, ASR & ROR
objectives: Combine a shift with a data-processing instruction
lessons.explanation: Practice tracing left shifts, logical right shifts, arithmetic right shifts, and rotates, including a shifted Operand2 inside another instruction.
examples:
MOV r0, #7; Load value 7
        MOV r1, r0, LSL #1; Shift left by 1 (multiply by 2)
        MOV r2, r1, LSR #2; Shift right by 2 (divide by 4)
        ADD r3, r0, r0, LSL #4; Multiply by 16 and add r0
commonMistakes: Assuming LSR and ASR are identical for values whose top bit is 1.
lessons.explain: Practice tracing left shifts, logical right shifts, arithmetic right shifts, and rotates, including a shifted Operand2 inside another instruction.

lessons.title: Flag-setting practice with the S suffix
objectives: Explain N, Z, C, and V
Use the S suffix to update flags
Separate signed overflow from unsigned carry
lessons.explanation: Practice instructions that update CPSR flags and trace the resulting N, Z, C, and V values.
examples:
MOV  r0, #5; Set initial value 5
        SUBS r1, r0, #5; Subtract 5 and update flags (Z=1)
        MOVS r2, #-1; Move -1 and update flags (N=1)
commonMistakes: Treating C and V as the same condition.
lessons.explain: Practice instructions that update CPSR flags and trace the resulting N, Z, C, and V values.

lessons.title: CMP, TST & conditional execution practice
objectives: Use comparison instructions to set flags
Choose a condition code from flag results
lessons.explanation: Practice setting flags with comparison or test instructions, then choosing the correct conditional instruction or branch.
examples:
MOV r0, #2; Load test value 2
        CMP r0, #2; Compare r0 with 2 (sets Z=1)
        MOVEQ r1, #1; Move 1 if equal (executed)
        MOVNE r1, #0; Move 0 if not equal (skipped)
        TST r0, #2; Bitwise test bit 1
commonMistakes: Expecting CMP to store a normal subtraction result.
lessons.explain: Practice setting flags with comparison or test instructions, then choosing the correct conditional instruction or branch.

lessons.title: Bit-manipulation practice
lessons.explanation: Practice using AND, ORR, EOR, and BIC with masks to keep, set, toggle, or clear selected bits.
examples:
MOV r0, #0x0F; Load bit mask 0x0F
        MOV r1, #0x03; Load bit mask 0x03
        AND r2, r0, r1; Bitwise AND: 0x03
        ORR r3, r0, #0x10; Bitwise OR: 0x1F
        EOR r4, r0, r1; Bitwise XOR: 0x0C
        BIC r5, r0, #0x03; Bit clear lower 2 bits: 0x0C
commonMistakes: Using arithmetic intuition for bit masks instead of tracing each bit position.
lessons.explain: Practice using AND, ORR, EOR, and BIC with masks to keep, set, toggle, or clear selected bits.

lessons.title: Arithmetic instruction practice
lessons.explanation: Practice three-operand arithmetic with ADD, ADC, SUB, SBC, RSB, and RSC, including carry-aware and reverse-subtraction cases.
examples:
MOV r1, #9; Load operand 1
        MOV r2, #4; Load operand 2
        ADD r0, r1, r2; Add: 9 + 4 = 13
        SUB r3, r1, r2; Subtract: 9 - 4 = 5
        RSB r4, r1, r2; Reverse subtract: 4 - 9 = -5
commonMistakes: Applying normal SUB operand order to RSB.
lessons.explain: Practice three-operand arithmetic with ADD, ADC, SUB, SBC, RSB, and RSC, including carry-aware and reverse-subtraction cases.

lessons.title: Branch, if/else & loop practice
lessons.explanation: Practice labels, conditional branches, if/else control flow, and loops by tracing the program counter and loop state.
examples:
j       RN 0; Alias register r0 as loop counter j
        MOV j, #3; Initialize counter j to 3
loop    CMP j, #0; Compare j with 0
        BLT done; Exit loop when j < 0
        SUB j, j, #1; Decrement counter
        B loop; Repeat loop
done    B done; Halt when loop finishes
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a loop must modify the state used by its termination condition.
lessons.explain: Practice labels, conditional branches, if/else control flow, and loops by tracing the program counter and loop state.

lessons.title: Stack & multiple-register transfer practice
lessons.explanation: Practice LDM/STM and PUSH/POP while tracing SP and the memory addresses used by each transfer.
examples:
LDR r3, =0x11111111; Load literal value 1
        LDR r4, =0x22222222; Load literal value 2
        PUSH {r3, r4}; Push r3 and r4 onto stack
        POP  {r5, r6}; Pop from stack into r5 and r6
commonMistakes: Assuming textual register-list order controls memory ordering.
lessons.explain: Practice LDM/STM and PUSH/POP while tracing SP and the memory addresses used by each transfer.

lessons.title: Subroutine & parameter-passing practice
objectives: Call and return from a subroutine
Compare register, memory-block, and stack parameter passing
lessons.explanation: Practice BL, BX LR, register preservation, and parameter passing by tracing calls and returns.
examples:
main    MOV r0, #5; Main function argument
        BL double; Branch with link to subroutine
        B stop; Halt execution

double  PUSH {r1}; Save caller register r1
        ADD r1, r0, r0; Double value in r0
        MOV r0, r1; Store return value in r0
        POP {r1}; Restore caller register r1
        BX lr; Return to caller
stop    B stop; Spin loop
commonMistakes: Calling another function without protecting LR when the current function still needs its own return address.
lessons.explain: Practice BL, BX LR, register preservation, and parameter passing by tracing calls and returns.

lessons.title: Exception-vector & handler practice
objectives: List major classic ARM exception types
lessons.explanation: Practice reading the classic ARM vector table and tracing how control reaches and returns from reset, SVC, IRQ, FIQ, and abort handlers.
examples:
0x00  Reset; Hardware reset entry point
0x04  Undefined instruction; Undefined instruction trap
0x08  SVC; Supervisor call software interrupt
0x0C  Prefetch abort; Instruction fetch memory fault
0x10  Data abort; Data access memory fault
0x18  IRQ; Standard priority hardware interrupt
0x1C  FIQ; Fast priority hardware interrupt
commonMistakes: Using the same unadjusted LR return sequence for every exception type.
lessons.explain: Practice reading the classic ARM vector table and tracing how control reaches and returns from reset, SVC, IRQ, FIQ, and abort handlers.

exercises.title: Arithmetic register trace

exercises.title: Bit-mask design
exercises.prompt: Use AND/ORR/EOR/BIC to test, set, toggle, and clear specified bits.

exercises.title: Shift and rotate trace
exercises.prompt: Trace LSL, LSR, ASR, and ROR on 32-bit patterns.

exercises.title: Flag prediction
exercises.prompt: Predict N, Z, C, and V for ADDS/SUBS-style operations.

exercises.title: Condition-code choice
exercises.prompt: Given CMP/TST results, choose a suitable condition code and explain why.

exercises.title: Translate a loop
exercises.prompt: Translate while or do-while pseudocode into ARM compare/branch structure.

exercises.title: Effective-address trace
exercises.prompt: Calculate addresses and base updates for pre/post-indexed LDR/STR.

exercises.title: Stack trace
exercises.prompt: Trace SP/register values through PUSH/POP and equivalent LDM/STM.

exercises.title: Function-call trace
exercises.prompt: Trace BL, LR, register preservation, parameters, and BX LR through nested calls.

exercises.title: Exception-entry trace
exercises.prompt: Given IRQ, FIQ, or SVC, list state changes, vector target, and return information.

projects.title: ARM instruction trace workbook
projects.description: Create documented ARM snippets covering arithmetic, masks, shifts, flags, and conditional execution. Predict state before checking it in the university simulator.
requirements: At least one edge case per instruction family

projects.title: Array & string routine pack
projects.description: Design ARM routines that traverse an integer array and a zero-terminated string using load/store addressing, loops, and clear calling conventions.
requirements: Preserve required registers and test boundary cases

projects.title: Function & stack lab
projects.description: Design a multi-function ARM program that passes parameters in registers and on the stack, preserves state, and traces SP/LR across nested calls.
requirements: Complete SP/LR trace and return reasoning

capstone.title: ARM assembly mini-runtime & interrupt design
capstone.description: Design a cohesive ARM assembly program combining data processing, memory access, loops, subroutines, stack discipline, and a documented exception/interrupt handler path.
requirements: Explicit calling convention and stack trace
Vector/handler design for at least one exception
Verification plan using the university ARM simulator

careerApplications: Useful for firmware, embedded systems, low-level debugging, reverse-engineering fundamentals, compiler/code-generation understanding, and computer engineering interviews.

quiz.q: AREA, ENTRY, EQU, and END are primarily:
quiz.explanation: AREA organizes a section, ENTRY marks an entry point, EQU defines a constant, and END ends the source. These direct the assembler rather than perform CPU calculations.

quiz.q: For a typical three-operand ARM data-processing instruction, the first register is usually:
quiz.explanation: In ADD r0, r1, r2, r0 receives the result while r1 and r2 supply values. Read the operands from destination to sources.
MOV r0, r1 reads r1 and writes its value into r0. r1 is unchanged.

options: The bitwise complement of its operand
quiz.explanation: MVN flips every bit of the source. In a 32-bit register, MVN applied to 0 gives 0xFFFFFFFF, not 1.
RSB reverses the usual SUB order: RSB r0, r1, r2 stores r2 minus r1 in r0.

options: A carry from a previous arithmetic step must be included
quiz.explanation: ADC computes operand1 + operand2 + C. This lets the carry from a low-word addition feed a high-word addition.
BIC computes operand1 AND NOT operand2. A 1 in the mask therefore clears the corresponding destination bit.
EOR sets a result bit when the two corresponding input bits differ; equal bits produce 0.

quiz.q: ASR differs from LSR because ASR:
options: Preserves the sign bit when shifting right
quiz.explanation: ASR replicates the top/sign bit while shifting right. LSR shifts zeros into the high positions.

options: Shift an operand as part of another data-processing instruction
quiz.explanation: ADD r0, r1, r2, LSL #2 shifts r2 left by two before adding it to r1. The shifted value need not be stored in a separate register.

quiz.q: The Z flag is set when the relevant result is:
quiz.explanation: Z is 1 when the flag-setting operation produces zero. A plain instruction without S usually leaves these flags unchanged.
V indicates that the mathematical signed result cannot fit in a signed 32-bit value. It is different from unsigned carry C.

options: Updates condition flags based on a subtraction-like comparison
quiz.explanation: CMP uses a subtraction to set NZCV but discards the arithmetic result. It does not overwrite either compared register.

quiz.q: TST primarily uses which logical operation for flag testing?
quiz.explanation: TST calculates a bitwise AND for the flags without saving that AND result in a destination register.

options: Condition flags and a condition code
quiz.explanation: The condition suffix reads flags set earlier. BEQ tests Z=1; BLT tests N different from V for a signed comparison.

quiz.q: A do-while style loop differs from a while loop because its body:
quiz.explanation: A do-while style loop places its test after the body, so the body runs at least once. A while style loop can skip the body when its first test fails.

options: Load data from memory into a register
quiz.explanation: LDR reads the word at an effective memory address and places it in the destination register. STR transfers a register value in the opposite direction.

options: Uses the current base address, then updates the base
Updates the base before the access only
quiz.explanation: LDR r0, [r1], #4 loads using the old address in r1, then increases r1 by four. The offset is outside the brackets.
PUSH preserves register values in memory on the stack and adjusts SP. It is useful before a subroutine changes values the caller needs.

quiz.q: In the stack convention shown in this course, the stack grows toward:
quiz.explanation: In the full descending convention, reserving stack space decreases SP; releasing it increases SP. Lower memory addresses hold newer stack entries.

quiz.q: BL does what in addition to branching?
options: Saves a return address in LR
quiz.explanation: BL saves the address of the instruction after the call in LR before transferring control. A nested call must preserve a needed earlier LR.

quiz.q: A simple subroutine commonly returns with:
quiz.explanation: BX LR branches to the saved return address. LR must still hold the intended return address for this to work.

quiz.q: On classic ARM exception entry, CPSR is copied into:
quiz.explanation: Classic ARM exception entry saves the old CPSR in the target mode SPSR so the handler can later restore the interrupted status. The tracer does not model exception entry.

options: Request a privileged software service by raising a software exception
quiz.explanation: SVC deliberately raises a software exception to request a supervisor service. It is not an ordinary BL subroutine call; handling depends on the execution environment.
